_README: R-8 §13. The human half of scripts/preflight.mjs.
Each key below is something no program can establish from inside a
process: a DNS record resolving, a certificate terminating, a restore
actually performed, an SMS reaching a handset, a push landing on a phone,
an alert waking a person, a school completing an onboarding. The preflight
checks whether the CONFIGURATION for each exists; this file records
whether the THING actually happened, and WHERE.
Shape, per R-8 §13:
status       null | "rehearsed" | "verified"
date         ISO date the observation was made
environment  the deployment it was observed on, verbatim
evidence     what was actually seen — numbers, not adjectives
result       "pass" | "fail"
THE ENVIRONMENT FIELD IS LOAD-BEARING. The preflight compares it against
the deployment being checked and treats a mismatch as UNVERIFIED. That is
deliberate: a restore rehearsed on a laptop is real work and worth
recording, and it is NOT a production restore. An evidence file that could
not tell those apart would let a rehearsal close a production gate, which
is the exact failure this mechanism exists to prevent.
Rules:
- null means never tested. Keep it null. A null is worth more than a
confident guess, and every one of these was null before it was earned.
- Never fill an entry from configuration intent. "The provider is
configured" is not "a message arrived".
- Attestations lapse after 180 days: "we restored a backup successfully"
stops being a fact about the current system fairly quickly.
- status "rehearsed" means the procedure was executed somewhere that is
not the target environment. It closes no production gate. It exists so
the production run is a repeat of a rehearsed thing rather than a first
attempt during an incident.

restore_drill.evidence: scripts/restore-drill.mjs against the local Postgres 16.15 container. pg_dump -Fc 2.6 MB in 0.6s; restored into an isolated database in 3.0s; 7 schema counts (121 tables, 355 indexes, 110 RLS-enabled tables, 227 policies, 86 functions, 162 triggers, 4 attendance partitions) and 27 table counts identical to the source; all 8 tenants identical across students, teachers, guardians, attendance, marks and invoices. RTO observed 4.0s on a 2.6 MB database. NOT a production restore: production is Neon and restores there are branch-based, with different failure modes. RPO is not measured by any drill — it is a property of the backup schedule.

prod_cross_tenant.evidence: scripts/security-probe.mjs — 29 of 29 checks across 12 areas against a running deployment, positive and negative cases, none failing, none skipped. Covers: positive control (roster, sync/pull, dashboard all serve the right school); forged X-Tenant-ID/X-User-ID/X-Role ignored in favour of signed claims; headers-without-token and garbage-bearer both 401; cross-tenant reads of section, student and attendance by id refused; a cross-tenant WRITE through a payload tenantId not applied; no runtime role holds SUPERUSER or BYPASSRLS; tenant A's DB context cannot see tenant B's rows by primary key while still seeing its own; no tenant context set means nothing visible; every table carrying tenant_id has RLS enabled; a service credential from a browser refused; a user token is not a service credential and cannot run maintenance; 7 hostile push endpoints (http, loopback, 169.254.169.254, private range, userinfo, .internal, .local) all refused; cross-tenant notice and document access refused; the platform health endpoint unreachable with a tenant token; the console refuses both a tenant user and an anonymous caller; no live secret value or connection string in app.js/platform.js/sw.js; error bodies carry no credential; an unlisted CORS origin is not echoed and credentials are never allowed; per-phone OTP requests are rate-limited. NOT run against production — no production deployment exists.
